facts.fact: Fish colour is mostly set by genetics, but fish cannot make red, orange, yellow, green and some blue pigments themselves; they get them from food.
Fish kept in aquariums or recirculating systems without pigment in their diet fade and lose their bright colours.
Plants and algae can make carotenoids but animals cannot, so carotenoid-based colour fades when the food lacks them.
In University of Hawaii trials, swordtails, rainbowfish, mollies and cichlids showed clearly stronger colours within one week of carotenoid feeding.
The colour gained from carotenoid additives faded again once the additives were stopped.
Different fish species process carotenoids differently.
Carotenes and astaxanthins strengthen yellowish and reddish tones in fish skin.
Metallic, shimmering (structural) colours depend on light, not pigment, and food does not change them (JBL).
Too much natural colourant in the feed can turn a white koi pink.
JBL says red koi need extra colour-enhancing ingredients, while orange koi and goldfish do not.
Carotenes come from sources such as carrots, and astaxanthins from prey animals such as krill and brine shrimp.
In a Ho Chi Minh City trial on about 6 cm Sahyadria denisonii, astaxanthin at 20, 30 or 40 mg/kg feed was fed for 90 days.
In that trial, redness (a* value) was highest at 40 mg/kg (5.53), then 30 mg/kg (3.45), 20 mg/kg (1.65) and the control (0.45).
The authors recommend 40 mg astaxanthin per kg feed for 3 months to improve the colour of Sahyadria denisonii.
In the Sahyadria denisonii trial, astaxanthin did not change survival or growth significantly.
The astaxanthin colour trial on Sahyadria denisonii was done by the Center for Research and Development of High-Tech Agriculture in Ho Chi Minh City (2022).
sera Discus Color Granules contain 175 mg astaxanthin per kg of food, from Haematococcus algae.
sera Discus Color Granules also contain 4% krill meal, 0.5% Gammarus meal, and paprika, spirulina, spinach and carrots.
sera advises feeding its discus colour food once or twice daily, only as much as the fish eat within a short time.
sera says its colour granules are meant to be fed alongside a staple food.
Discus have a short gut, so sera advises feeding sparingly and using food that does not swell in the stomach.
Discus can be fussy eaters and may need to be switched to a new food gradually.
Fish need ascorbic acid (vitamin C) delivered in their feed, and most fish feeds should be supplemented with a stabilized form.
Many fish cannot make vitamin C because they lack the enzyme L-gulonolactone oxidase.
Most commercial feed ingredients contain little or no vitamin C, and it breaks down by oxidation during processing and storage.
Vitamin C deficiency causes 'broken back disease'; severely affected fish show extreme scoliosis.
Bent or deformed gill cartilage seen on a wet mount at the 10× objective may point to past vitamin C deficiency.
Vitamin C deficiency signs include lordosis, scoliosis, deformed opercula and gill lamellae, bleeding, and slow wound healing.
Bleeding from vitamin C deficiency is often preceded by reduced appetite and lethargy.
Spinal deformities seen on X-ray may also come from injury or genetics, not only vitamin C deficiency.
Vitamin C deficiency is treated by vitamin C supplementation, taking losses during feed processing and storage into account.
More stable forms of vitamin C, with phosphate or sulfate attached, have been developed to reduce losses.
Vitamin C-deficient fish are more prone to bacterial infections, so infections should be dealt with promptly.
Poor nutrition can cause poor growth, deformities, a weaker immune system, fatty liver (hepatic lipidosis) and impaired metabolism.
Fatty liver can result from starvation, too much carbohydrate or fat in the diet, or rancid feed.
Feed a variety of live and commercial foods.
Adult fish need about 3% of body weight daily for maintenance; fry and fingerlings up to 5%.
Store dry feed in a pest-proof container in a cool, low-humidity place.
High heat and humidity degrade feed and cause mould, possible mycotoxins and rancidity.
Throw away opened feed kept at room temperature after 2 months, and commercial feed stored frozen after 6 months.
Throw away commercial frozen foods (brine shrimp, bloodworms, mysids, glassworms) after 1 year.
Do not refreeze frozen feed after it has thawed.
Bottom dwellers such as loricariids and Corydoras should be target-fed, not left to eat leftovers.
Brine shrimp eggs hatch best at about 80–84°F; below 78°F hatching can take up to 36 hours, and above about 86°F the nauplii suffocate.
Lange and Hellweg's hatching brine is 2 tablespoons of salt and 1 teaspoon of Epsom salt in 1.4 liters of warm water (specific gravity about 1.019).
The hatching water should be pH 8 or higher; with soft water, about ¼ teaspoon of baking soda per liter may be needed.
Most brine shrimp eggs hatch within 18–24 hours.
Lange and Hellweg add three drops of unscented chlorine bleach to kill contaminants on the egg casings, instead of full decapsulation.
Newly hatched nauplii do not feed and live on their fat; by the end of the first instar their body fat can drop by up to 39%.
Nauplii are most nutritious in about the first 12 hours, so hatch fresh ones daily instead of storing them.
UF/IFAS fact sheet FA024 by Rottmann, Graves, Watson and Yanong covers culturing Moina (water fleas) as food for freshwater fish fry.
The Moina fact sheet points to Moina's high reproduction rate and tolerance of varied conditions as advantages for culture.
A Parosphromenus Project post says Moina macrocopa is the species most often recommended for culture.
Vietnamese shop blogs list artemia, trùn chỉ (tubifex), trùn huyết (bloodworm), lăng quăng (mosquito larvae), bo bo (Moina) and tảo xoắn (spirulina) as colour foods.
In Vietnam, colour-enhancing pellets are sold as 'cám tăng màu', e.g. IPick koi food labelled 'Tăng Trọng Tăng Màu'.
Vietnamese names: 'cá dĩa' = discus (Symphysodon); 'thức ăn kích màu' = colour-enhancing food.
Vietnamese names: 'trứng artemia' = Artemia cysts; 'ấu trùng' = nauplii; 'tách vỏ trứng' = decapsulation; 'cá bột' = fry.
Vietnamese names: 'bo bo' = Moina; 'rận nước' = Daphnia; 'trùng bánh xe' = rotifer.
